title: Vector Spaces & Eigenvalues
description: Span, independence, bases, dimension, rank–nullity, linear transformations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalization, orthogonality, Gram–Schmidt, least squares and the SVD.

cards.title: What three conditions make a subset $H$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ a subspace?
cards.body:
$H$ contains $\mathbf{0}$, is **closed under addition** ($\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in H \Rightarrow \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \in H$), and is closed under scalar multiplication ($\mathbf{u} \in H \Rightarrow c\mathbf{u} \in H$).

Tip: Checking for $\mathbf{0}$ first is the fastest way to rule a set out.
cards.searchQuery: subspace test three conditions zero vector closure

cards.title: Is the line $y = 2x + 1$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$?
cards.body:
No: it doesn't contain the **zero vector**, since $0 \neq 2(0) + 1$.

The subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^2$ are $\{\mathbf{0}\}$, the lines through the origin and $\mathbb{R}^2$ itself.

Key idea: The parallel line $y = 2x$ is a subspace.
cards.searchQuery: line y=2x+1 not a subspace zero vector

cards.title: Is $\{(x, y) : xy \geq 0\}$, the first and third quadrants with the axes, a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$?
cards.body:
No: it is **not closed under addition**.

Example: $(1, 0)$ and $(0, -1)$ are both in the set, but their sum $(1, -1)$ has $xy = -1 < 0$.
Watch out: The set does contain $\mathbf{0}$ and is closed under scalar multiples, so all three conditions really must be checked.
cards.searchQuery: first and third quadrants not a subspace closure under addition

cards.title: $U$ and $W$ are subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Which is always a subspace: $U \cap W$ or $U \cup W$?
cards.body:
The **intersection** $U \cap W$.

Example: The union usually fails closure under addition: the $x$-axis $\cup$ the $y$-axis contains $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ but not $(1, 1)$.
Key idea: A union is a subspace only when one of the two contains the other.
cards.searchQuery: union of subspaces not a subspace intersection is

cards.title: Is the set of polynomials of degree exactly $2$ a vector space under the usual operations?
cards.body:
No.

It has no **zero vector** (the zero polynomial doesn't have degree $2$), and it isn't closed under addition: $(t^2 + t) + (-t^2) = t$.

Key idea: The polynomials of degree at most $2$, $\mathbb{P}_2$, do form a vector space.
cards.searchQuery: polynomials of degree exactly 2 not a vector space

cards.title: What is the dimension of $\mathbb{P}_3$, the space of polynomials of degree at most $3$?
cards.body:
$4$.

The **standard basis** is $\{1, t, t^2, t^3\}$.

Watch out: In general $\dim \mathbb{P}_n = n + 1$; the common slip is forgetting the constant polynomial $1$.
cards.searchQuery: dimension of P3 polynomials degree at most 3

cards.title: What is the dimension of the space of symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrices?
cards.body:
$6$.

A symmetric matrix is determined by its entries **on and above the diagonal**: $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$.

Key idea: In general the dimension is $\tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$, while all $n \times n$ matrices form a space of dimension $n^2$.
cards.searchQuery: dimension of symmetric 3x3 matrices

cards.title: What is $\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_p\}$?
cards.body:
The set of all **linear combinations** $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{v}_p$, with $c_1, \dots, c_p$ any scalars.

Key idea: It is always a subspace, the smallest one containing $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_p$, and it always contains $\mathbf{0}$ (take every $c_i = 0$).
cards.searchQuery: span of vectors definition linear combinations

cards.title: Nonzero vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are not multiples of each other. What is $\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}\}$ geometrically?
cards.body:
A **plane through the origin**.

If $\mathbf{v}$ were a multiple of $\mathbf{u}$, the span would collapse to a line through the origin.

Key idea: Two vectors can never span all of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
cards.searchQuery: span of two vectors in R3 plane through origin

cards.title: When is a set of vectors $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_p\}$ linearly independent?
cards.body:
When $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{v}_p = \mathbf{0}$ has only the **trivial solution** $c_1 = \cdots = c_p = 0$.

Key idea: If some nontrivial combination gives $\mathbf{0}$, that equation is a linear dependence relation and the set is dependent.
cards.searchQuery: linearly independent definition trivial solution only

cards.title: How do you test whether the columns of a matrix $A$ are linearly independent?
cards.body:
Row reduce $A$: the columns are independent iff **every column is a pivot column**.

Equivalently, $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution.

Key idea: Any free variable gives a dependence relation among the columns.
cards.searchQuery: test linear independence of columns pivot columns

cards.title: Can a set of vectors that contains the zero vector be linearly independent?
cards.body:
No.

Why: If $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{0}$, then $1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 + 0 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + 0 \cdot \mathbf{v}_p = \mathbf{0}$ is a **nontrivial dependence relation**.
cards.searchQuery: set containing zero vector linearly dependent

cards.title: Can $5$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^4$ be linearly independent?
cards.body:
No.

As columns they form a $4 \times 5$ matrix with at most $4$ pivots, so some column has no pivot and $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has a **nontrivial solution**.

Key idea: In $\mathbb{R}^n$, any set of more than $n$ vectors is dependent.
cards.searchQuery: more than n vectors in R^n linearly dependent

cards.title: For what value of $h$ are $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ h \end{pmatrix}$ linearly dependent?
cards.body:
$h = 2$.

The **determinant** of the matrix with these columns is $h - 2$, which is $0$ only at $h = 2$.

Tip: at $h = 2$ the third vector is the sum of the first two.
cards.searchQuery: linearly dependent vectors parameter h determinant

cards.title: A set of two or more vectors is linearly dependent. What must be true of the vectors themselves?
cards.body:
**At least one** of them is a linear combination of the others.

Watch out: Not necessarily every one: in $\{(1, 0), (2, 0), (0, 1)\}$, the vector $(0, 1)$ is not a combination of the other two.
Key idea: For exactly two vectors, dependent means one is a scalar multiple of the other.
cards.searchQuery: linearly dependent set one vector combination of others

cards.title: $\mathbf{v}_3$ is a linear combination of $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$. Does adding $\mathbf{v}_3$ to the set $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\}$ change its span?
cards.body:
No, the **span stays the same**.

Any combination that uses $\mathbf{v}_3$ can be rewritten with $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ alone.

Key idea: Deleting redundant vectors from a spanning set, one at a time, leaves a basis (the spanning set theorem).
cards.searchQuery: redundant vector does not change span spanning set theorem

cards.title: What is a basis for a subspace $H$?
cards.body:
A **linearly independent** set of vectors in $H$ that spans $H$.

Key idea: Every vector in $H$ is then a combination of the basis vectors in exactly one way.
cards.searchQuery: basis definition linearly independent spanning set

cards.title: What is the dimension of a nonzero subspace $H$, and why is it well defined?
cards.body:
The number of vectors in a basis of $H$.

It is well defined because **every basis** of $H$ has the same number of vectors.

Key idea: By convention $\dim\{\mathbf{0}\} = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: dimension of a subspace number of basis vectors

cards.title: $V$ has dimension $p$. When is a set of exactly $p$ vectors in $V$ a basis?
cards.body:
When it is linearly independent, or when it spans $V$: with exactly $p$ vectors, **either property implies the other**.

Tip: This halves the work of checking a basis.
Key idea: Fewer than $p$ vectors can't span $V$, and more than $p$ can't be independent.
cards.searchQuery: basis theorem p vectors in p-dimensional space

cards.title: In what sense is a basis both as small and as large as possible?
cards.body:
It is a spanning set that is **as small as possible** and an independent set that is as large as possible.

Key idea: Remove a vector and the set no longer spans; add any vector and the set is no longer independent.
cards.searchQuery: basis minimal spanning set maximal independent set

cards.title: $\mathcal{B} = \{(1, 1), (1, -1)\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$. What is the coordinate vector of $\mathbf{x} = (5, 1)$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$?
cards.searchQuery: coordinate vector relative to a basis example

cards.title: $P_{\mathcal{B}} = [\,\mathbf{b}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{b}_n\,]$ holds a basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$. How are $\mathbf{x}$ and $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ related?
cards.body:
$\mathbf{x} = P_{\mathcal{B}}[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$, so $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}$.

Multiplying by $P_{\mathcal{B}}$ **rebuilds** $\mathbf{x}$ from its weights on the basis vectors.

Why: $P_{\mathcal{B}}$ is invertible because its columns form a basis.
cards.searchQuery: change of coordinates matrix coordinate vector basis

cards.title: What is the dimension of the subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$ defined by $x + 2y - z = 0$?
cards.body:
$2$.

It is the null space of $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$: one pivot and two **free variables** ($y$ and $z$), giving the basis $\{(-2, 1, 0), (1, 0, 1)\}$.

Key idea: Geometrically, it is a plane through the origin.
cards.searchQuery: dimension of plane x+2y-z=0 null space

cards.title: What are the subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^3$, sorted by dimension?
cards.body:
Dimension $0$: $\{\mathbf{0}\}$. Dimension $1$: lines **through the origin**. Dimension $2$: planes through the origin. Dimension $3$: $\mathbb{R}^3$ itself.

Watch out: Lines and planes that miss the origin are not subspaces.
cards.searchQuery: subspaces of R3 by dimension lines planes

cards.title: What is the null space $\operatorname{Nul}A$ of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, and where does it live?
cards.body:
$\operatorname{Nul}A = \{\mathbf{x} : A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\}$, a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Tip: Its dimension is the number of **free variables** in $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, and the parametric vector form of the solution gives a basis.
cards.searchQuery: null space definition Nul A subspace of R^n

cards.title: What is the column space $\operatorname{Col}A$ of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, and where does it live?
cards.body:
The **span of the columns** of $A$, which equals $\{A\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\}$, a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m$.

Key idea: So $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is consistent exactly when $\mathbf{b}$ is in $\operatorname{Col}A$.
cards.searchQuery: column space Col A definition subspace of R^m

cards.title: To get a basis for $\operatorname{Col}A$ you locate the pivot columns. Do you then take those columns from $A$ or from its echelon form?
cards.body:
From $A$ itself.

Row operations change the column space: the columns of an echelon form usually don't even lie in $\operatorname{Col}A$.

Watch out: The echelon form only tells you **which columns to keep**.
Tip: for $\operatorname{Row}A$ it's the opposite: the nonzero rows of the echelon form work.
cards.searchQuery: basis for column space pivot columns of original matrix

cards.title: How do you find a basis for the row space of $A$?
cards.body:
Take the **nonzero rows** of any echelon form of $A$.

Why: Row operations replace rows with combinations of rows, so they don't change the row space, and the nonzero rows of an echelon form are linearly independent.
cards.searchQuery: basis for row space nonzero rows echelon form

cards.title: State the rank–nullity theorem for an $m \times n$ matrix $A$.
cards.body:
$\operatorname{rank}A + \dim\operatorname{Nul}A = n$, the **number of columns**.

Pivot columns plus free-variable columns account for every column.

Watch out: The total is $n$ (columns), not $m$ (rows): a classic slip.
cards.searchQuery: rank-nullity theorem rank plus nullity equals columns

cards.title: A $5 \times 7$ matrix has rank $3$. What is the dimension of its null space?
cards.body:
$4$.

**Rank–nullity**: $\dim\operatorname{Nul}A = n - \operatorname{rank}A = 7 - 3$, using the $7$ columns.

Watch out: Using the $5$ rows instead gives the wrong answer $2$.
cards.searchQuery: rank nullity 5x7 matrix rank 3 nullity

cards.title: What is the smallest possible dimension of $\operatorname{Nul}A$ for a $4 \times 6$ matrix $A$?
cards.body:
$2$.

The rank is at most $4$ (**at most one pivot per row**), so $\dim\operatorname{Nul}A = 6 - \operatorname{rank}A \geq 2$.

Key idea: A matrix with more columns than rows always has a nontrivial null space.
cards.searchQuery: smallest nullity of a 4 by 6 matrix

cards.title: $A$ is a $5 \times 3$ matrix of rank $3$. What is the dimension of $\operatorname{Nul}A^T$?
cards.body:
$2$.

$A^T$ is $3 \times 5$ with rank $3$, so $\dim\operatorname{Nul}A^T = 5 - 3$.

Key idea: For any $m \times n$ matrix of rank $r$: $\dim\operatorname{Col}A = \dim\operatorname{Row}A = r$, $\dim\operatorname{Nul}A = n - r$ and $\dim\operatorname{Nul}A^T = m - r$.
cards.searchQuery: dimension of left null space Nul A transpose

cards.title: Why does $\dim\operatorname{Row}A = \dim\operatorname{Col}A$ for every matrix $A$?
cards.body:
Both equal the **number of pivots** in an echelon form of $A$.

The pivot columns of $A$ form a basis for $\operatorname{Col}A$, and the nonzero rows of the echelon form (one per pivot) form a basis for $\operatorname{Row}A$.

Key idea: So $\operatorname{rank}A = \operatorname{rank}A^T$.
cards.searchQuery: row rank equals column rank number of pivots

cards.title: $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ are nonzero. What is the rank of $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T$?
cards.body:
$1$.

Column $j$ of $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T$ is $v_j\mathbf{u}$, so every column is a **multiple of** $\mathbf{u}$, and at least one is nonzero.

Key idea: Conversely, every rank-$1$ matrix can be written as $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T$.
cards.searchQuery: rank of outer product u v transpose is one

cards.title: How does $\operatorname{rank}(A^TA)$ compare with $\operatorname{rank}A$?
cards.body:
They are equal.

$A^TA$ and $A$ have the **same null space**: if $A^TA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, then $\mathbf{x}^TA^TA\mathbf{x} = \|A\mathbf{x}\|^2 = 0$, so $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$.

Why: Both have $n$ columns, so rank–nullity gives equal ranks.
Key idea: Hence $A^TA$ is invertible iff $A$ has independent columns.
cards.searchQuery: rank of A transpose A equals rank of A

cards.title: How does $\operatorname{rank}(AB)$ compare with $\operatorname{rank}A$ and $\operatorname{rank}B$?
cards.body:
$\operatorname{rank}(AB) \leq \min(\operatorname{rank}A, \operatorname{rank}B)$.

The columns of $AB$ are combinations of the columns of $A$, so $\operatorname{Col}(AB) \subseteq \operatorname{Col}A$; likewise the rows of $AB$ are combinations of the rows of $B$.

Key idea: Multiplying can **never raise the rank**.
cards.searchQuery: rank of a product at most min of ranks

cards.title: What two properties make $T: V \to W$ a linear transformation?
cards.body:
$T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v})$ and $T(c\mathbf{u}) = cT(\mathbf{u})$ for all vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$ and scalars $c$.

Together they say $T$ **preserves linear combinations**.

Key idea: A consequence: $T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$.
cards.searchQuery: linear transformation two properties additivity homogeneity

cards.title: Is $T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{0}$ a linear transformation?
cards.body:
No: $T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{0}$, but every linear map sends $\mathbf{0}$ to $\mathbf{0}$.

Key idea: Translations, and **affine maps** $A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{0}$, are not linear.
Tip: Checking $T(\mathbf{0})$ is the quickest test.
cards.searchQuery: translation not a linear transformation T(0) nonzero

cards.title: How do you find the standard matrix of a linear transformation $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$?
cards.body:
Its columns are $T(\mathbf{e}_1), T(\mathbf{e}_2), \dots, T(\mathbf{e}_n)$, the images of the **standard basis vectors**.

Key idea: Then $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ for every $\mathbf{x}$, because $\mathbf{x} = x_1\mathbf{e}_1 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{e}_n$ and $T$ preserves linear combinations.
cards.searchQuery: standard matrix of linear transformation columns images of e_i

cards.title: What is the standard matrix of the counterclockwise rotation of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by an angle $\theta$?
cards.body:
$\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}$

Column 1 is where $\mathbf{e}_1$ lands, $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$; column 2 is where $\mathbf{e}_2$ lands, $(-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$.

Key idea: A rotation **preserves lengths** and has determinant $1$.
cards.searchQuery: rotation matrix in R2 counterclockwise angle theta

cards.title: What is the standard matrix of the reflection of $\mathbb{R}^2$ across the line $y = x$?
cards.body:
$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$

It **swaps the coordinates**: $\mathbf{e}_1 \mapsto \mathbf{e}_2$ and $\mathbf{e}_2 \mapsto \mathbf{e}_1$.

Key idea: Like every reflection, it has determinant $-1$, and applying it twice gives $I$.
cards.searchQuery: reflection matrix across line y=x

cards.title: When is the linear map $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ one-to-one?
cards.body:
Exactly when $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution, i.e., when the columns of $A$ are **linearly independent**.

Why: If $T(\mathbf{u}) = T(\mathbf{v})$, then $A(\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}$, so a trivial null space forces $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}$.
Tip: In pivot terms: every column is a pivot column.
cards.searchQuery: linear map one-to-one columns linearly independent

cards.title: $A$ is $m \times n$. When does the linear map $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ map onto $\mathbb{R}^m$?
cards.body:
Exactly when the columns of $A$ span $\mathbb{R}^m$, i.e., when $A$ has a **pivot in every row**.

Key idea: Onto means every $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ equals $A\mathbf{x}$ for some $\mathbf{x}$, so $\operatorname{Col}A = \mathbb{R}^m$ and $\operatorname{rank}A = m$.
cards.searchQuery: linear map onto columns span R^m pivot in every row

cards.title: Can a linear transformation $T: \mathbb{R}^5 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be one-to-one?
cards.body:
No.

Its $3 \times 5$ standard matrix has rank at most $3$, so its null space has dimension at least $5 - 3 = 2$: **some nonzero vectors** are sent to $\mathbf{0}$.

Key idea: Likewise, a linear map $\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^5$ can never be onto.
cards.searchQuery: linear map R5 to R3 cannot be one-to-one

cards.title: $S$ has standard matrix $A$ and $T$ has standard matrix $B$. What is the standard matrix of $T \circ S$ (apply $S$ first)?
cards.body:
$BA$.

$(T \circ S)(\mathbf{x}) = T(S(\mathbf{x})) = B(A\mathbf{x}) = (BA)\mathbf{x}$.

Watch out: The matrix of the map applied first **sits on the right**, next to $\mathbf{x}$.
cards.searchQuery: matrix of composition of linear maps order BA

cards.title: What is the matrix of $D = \frac{d}{dt}$ on $\mathbb{P}_2$ relative to the basis $\{1, t, t^2\}$?
cards.body:
$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$

Column $j$ holds the **coordinates** of $D$ applied to basis vector $j$: $D(1) = 0$, $D(t) = 1$, $D(t^2) = 2t$.

Key idea: Its null space (the constants) is nonzero, so $D$ is not invertible.
cards.searchQuery: matrix of derivative on P2 standard basis

cards.title: What are an eigenvector and an eigenvalue of a square matrix $A$?
cards.body:
An eigenvector is a **nonzero** $\mathbf{v}$ with $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ for some scalar $\lambda$, and that $\lambda$ is its eigenvalue.

$A$ only stretches, shrinks or flips an eigenvector along its own line.

Watch out: The zero vector is never an eigenvector, but $\lambda = 0$ can be an eigenvalue.
cards.searchQuery: eigenvector eigenvalue definition Av = lambda v

cards.title: Which equation do you solve to find the eigenvalues of a square matrix $A$?
cards.body:
The characteristic equation $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$.

Why: $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$ means $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ has a nontrivial solution, which happens exactly when $A - \lambda I$ is **singular**.
cards.searchQuery: characteristic equation det(A - lambda I) = 0 eigenvalues

cards.title: What are the eigenvalues of $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$?
cards.body:
$\lambda = 2$ and $\lambda = 5$.

For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, $\det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr}A)\lambda + \det A = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 5)$.

Tip: verify: $2 + 5 = 7$ is the **trace** and $2 \cdot 5 = 10$ is the determinant.
cards.searchQuery: eigenvalues of 2x2 matrix trace determinant

cards.title: Find an eigenvector of $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ for the eigenvalue $\lambda = 5$.
cards.body:
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, or **any nonzero multiple** of it.

$A - 5I = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, so $-x + y = 0$.

Tip: verify: $A\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$.
cards.searchQuery: find eigenvector for eigenvalue null space A minus lambda I

cards.title: What are the eigenvalues of $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 7 & -1 \\ 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$?
cards.body:
$3$, $-2$ and $5$: the **diagonal entries**.

$A - \lambda I$ is still triangular, so $\det(A - \lambda I) = (3 - \lambda)(-2 - \lambda)(5 - \lambda)$.

Watch out: This shortcut works only for triangular (or diagonal) matrices.
cards.searchQuery: eigenvalues of triangular matrix diagonal entries

cards.title: $0$ is an eigenvalue of a square matrix $A$. Is $A$ invertible?
cards.body:
No.

$\lambda = 0$ means $A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for some $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$, so $A$ has a **nontrivial null space** and $\det A = 0$.

Key idea: Conversely, $A$ is invertible exactly when $0$ is not an eigenvalue.
cards.searchQuery: zero eigenvalue implies singular matrix

cards.title: A $2 \times 2$ matrix has trace $7$ and one eigenvalue equal to $3$. What is the other eigenvalue?
cards.body:
$4$.

Key idea: The trace equals the **sum of the eigenvalues**, counted with multiplicity: $3 + \lambda_2 = 7$.
cards.searchQuery: trace equals sum of eigenvalues find missing eigenvalue

cards.title: A $3 \times 3$ matrix has eigenvalues $1$, $-2$ and $4$. What is its determinant?
cards.body:
$-8$.

The determinant is the **product of the eigenvalues**, counted with multiplicity: $1 \cdot (-2) \cdot 4$.

Tip: the trace is their sum, $3$.
cards.searchQuery: determinant equals product of eigenvalues

cards.title: What is the eigenspace of $A$ for an eigenvalue $\lambda$?
cards.body:
$\operatorname{Nul}(A - \lambda I)$: all eigenvectors for $\lambda$, together with $\mathbf{0}$.

It is a subspace, and its dimension is the **geometric multiplicity** of $\lambda$.

Tip: Find a basis by row reducing $A - \lambda I$.
cards.searchQuery: eigenspace definition null space geometric multiplicity

cards.title: $A\mathbf{v} = 3\mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$. What is the eigenvalue of $A^2 - 2A + I$ for the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$?
cards.body:
$4$.

$A^2\mathbf{v} = 9\mathbf{v}$, so $(A^2 - 2A + I)\mathbf{v} = (9 - 6 + 1)\mathbf{v}$.

Key idea: In general, if $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ then $p(A)\mathbf{v} = p(\lambda)\mathbf{v}$ for any polynomial $p$, with the **same eigenvector**.
cards.searchQuery: eigenvalue of polynomial in a matrix p(lambda)

cards.title: $A$ is invertible and has eigenvalue $4$. What is the corresponding eigenvalue of $A^{-1}$?
cards.body:
$\tfrac{1}{4}$, with the **same eigenvector**.

Why: Multiply $A\mathbf{v} = 4\mathbf{v}$ by $A^{-1}$: $\mathbf{v} = 4A^{-1}\mathbf{v}$, so $A^{-1}\mathbf{v} = \tfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{v}$.
cards.searchQuery: eigenvalue of inverse matrix reciprocal

cards.title: Eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k$ of $A$ correspond to distinct eigenvalues. What can you conclude about them?
cards.body:
They are **linearly independent**.

Key idea: So an $n \times n$ matrix has at most $n$ distinct eigenvalues, and if it has $n$ distinct real eigenvalues, its eigenvectors form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
cards.searchQuery: eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues linearly independent

cards.title: What are the algebraic and geometric multiplicities of an eigenvalue, and which is larger?
cards.body:
Algebraic: its multiplicity as a root of the characteristic polynomial. Geometric: the dimension of its eigenspace.

Key idea: Always $1 \leq$ **geometric** $\leq$ algebraic.
Watch out: When the geometric multiplicity is strictly smaller for some eigenvalue, the matrix is not diagonalizable.
cards.searchQuery: algebraic versus geometric multiplicity of eigenvalue

cards.title: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. What is the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue $3$?
cards.body:
$2$.

$A - 3I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has rank $1$, so its **null space has dimension** $3 - 1 = 2$.

Key idea: The algebraic multiplicity is $3$, so $A$ is not diagonalizable.
cards.searchQuery: geometric multiplicity of eigenvalue rank of A minus lambda I

cards.title: What are the eigenvalues of the $90^\circ$ rotation matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$?
cards.body:
$\lambda = \pm i$.

The characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2 + 1$, which has no real roots: a $90^\circ$ rotation leaves no real direction fixed.

Watch out: complex eigenvalues of a real matrix always come in **conjugate pairs** $a \pm bi$.
cards.searchQuery: eigenvalues of 90 degree rotation matrix complex

cards.title: $B = P^{-1}AP$ for an invertible $P$. Do $A$ and $B$ have the same eigenvalues? The same eigenvectors?
cards.body:
Same eigenvalues (in fact the **same characteristic polynomial**), but generally different eigenvectors.

If $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$, then $B(P^{-1}\mathbf{v}) = \lambda P^{-1}\mathbf{v}$.

Key idea: Similar matrices represent the same linear map in different bases, so they also share the determinant, trace and rank.
cards.searchQuery: similar matrices same eigenvalues characteristic polynomial

cards.title: Can you read the eigenvalues of $A$ off the diagonal of an echelon form of $A$?
cards.body:
No: **row operations change eigenvalues**.

$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$, but one row swap turns it into $I$, whose only eigenvalue is $1$.

Watch out: The diagonal shortcut applies only to $A$ itself, and only when $A$ is triangular.
cards.searchQuery: row operations change eigenvalues echelon form diagonal

cards.title: What does the Cayley–Hamilton theorem say?
cards.body:
Every square matrix **satisfies its own characteristic equation**: if $p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$, then $p(A) = 0$.

Example: For $2 \times 2$ matrices: $A^2 - (\operatorname{tr}A)A + (\det A)I = 0$.
Watch out: The tempting one-line proof $\det(A - A I) = 0$ is invalid: it produces a number, not a matrix.
cards.searchQuery: Cayley-Hamilton theorem matrix satisfies characteristic equation

cards.title: What does it mean for a square matrix $A$ to be diagonalizable?
cards.body:
$A = PDP^{-1}$ for some invertible $P$ and diagonal $D$; that is, $A$ is **similar to a diagonal matrix**.

Key idea: In the basis formed by the columns of $P$, the map $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ just scales each coordinate.
cards.searchQuery: diagonalizable matrix definition PDP inverse

cards.title: When is an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ diagonalizable, and how do you build $P$ and $D$?
cards.body:
Exactly when $A$ has $n$ **linearly independent eigenvectors**.

Put those eigenvectors in the columns of $P$, and their eigenvalues on the diagonal of $D$ in the same order.

Tip: Then $AP = PD$, so $A = PDP^{-1}$.
cards.searchQuery: diagonalization theorem n independent eigenvectors P and D

cards.title: A $3 \times 3$ matrix has three distinct real eigenvalues. Is it diagonalizable?
cards.body:
Yes.

Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are **independent**, so there are $3$ independent eigenvectors.

Watch out: The condition is sufficient but not necessary: $I_3$ has the single eigenvalue $1$ and is already diagonal.
cards.searchQuery: three distinct eigenvalues diagonalizable sufficient not necessary

cards.title: Why is $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ not diagonalizable?
cards.body:
Its only eigenvalue, $2$, has a **one-dimensional eigenspace**, so there aren't $2$ independent eigenvectors.

Why: $A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has rank $1$, so the eigenspace is spanned by $(1, 0)$ alone: algebraic multiplicity $2$, geometric multiplicity $1$.
cards.searchQuery: why shear matrix not diagonalizable eigenspace dimension

cards.title: In terms of multiplicities, when is a matrix with all real eigenvalues diagonalizable?
cards.body:
When every eigenvalue's **geometric multiplicity** equals its algebraic multiplicity.

Equivalently, the dimensions of the eigenspaces add up to $n$.

Watch out: A single deficient eigenvalue is enough to block diagonalization.
cards.searchQuery: diagonalizable geometric equals algebraic multiplicity

cards.title: $A = PDP^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal. What is $A^k$?
cards.body:
$PD^kP^{-1}$.

The **inner factors cancel**: $A^2 = PDP^{-1}PDP^{-1} = PD^2P^{-1}$, and so on.

Tip: $D^k$ is easy: raise each diagonal entry to the $k$th power.
cards.searchQuery: matrix power via diagonalization A^k = P D^k P inverse

cards.title: Diagonalize $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$: find $P$ and $D$ with $A = PDP^{-1}$.
cards.body:
$P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $D = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$

The **eigenvalues** are the diagonal entries $2$ and $-1$. $\operatorname{Nul}(A - 2I)$ gives $(1, 0)$ and $\operatorname{Nul}(A + I)$ gives $(1, -1)$.

Tip: Nonzero multiples of these columns also work, as long as each column stays matched with its eigenvalue in $D$.
cards.searchQuery: diagonalize 2x2 matrix example find P and D

cards.title: Is every diagonalizable matrix invertible? Is every invertible matrix diagonalizable?
cards.body:
No to both: the two properties are **independent**.

$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ is diagonal but singular, and $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is invertible but not diagonalizable.

Key idea: Invertibility is about whether $0$ is an eigenvalue; diagonalizability is about having enough eigenvectors.
cards.searchQuery: diagonalizable versus invertible independent properties

cards.title: What is the orthogonal complement $W^\perp$ of a subspace $W$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$?
cards.body:
The set of all vectors **orthogonal to every vector** in $W$.

$W^\perp$ is a subspace, $\dim W + \dim W^\perp = n$, and $(W^\perp)^\perp = W$.

Tip: To test membership, it's enough to check orthogonality to a spanning set of $W$.
cards.searchQuery: orthogonal complement definition dimension W perp

cards.title: For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, what is $(\operatorname{Row}A)^\perp$?
cards.body:
$\operatorname{Nul}A$.

$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ says exactly that $\mathbf{x}$ is **orthogonal to every row** of $A$.

Key idea: Applying this to $A^T$ gives $(\operatorname{Col}A)^\perp = \operatorname{Nul}A^T$.
cards.searchQuery: orthogonal complement of row space is null space

cards.title: Why is an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors linearly independent?
cards.body:
**Dot** a dependence relation $c_1\mathbf{u}_1 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{u}_p = \mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{u}_j$: every term but one vanishes, leaving $c_j(\mathbf{u}_j \cdot \mathbf{u}_j) = 0$.

Key idea: Since $\mathbf{u}_j \neq \mathbf{0}$, $\mathbf{u}_j \cdot \mathbf{u}_j > 0$, so $c_j = 0$ for every $j$.
cards.searchQuery: orthogonal set of nonzero vectors linearly independent proof

cards.title: $\{\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_p\}$ is an orthogonal basis for $W$ and $\mathbf{y} \in W$. In $\mathbf{y} = c_1\mathbf{u}_1 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{u}_p$, what is $c_j$?
cards.body:
$c_j = \dfrac{\mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_j}{\mathbf{u}_j \cdot \mathbf{u}_j}$

**No row reduction needed**: dot both sides with $\mathbf{u}_j$ and the other terms vanish.

Tip: For an orthonormal basis this is just $c_j = \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_j$.
cards.searchQuery: weights in orthogonal basis expansion formula

cards.title: $Q$ is a square matrix with orthonormal columns. What is $Q^{-1}$?
cards.body:
$Q^{-1} = Q^T$.

The $(i, j)$ entry of $Q^TQ$ is $\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{q}_j$, which is $1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise, so $Q^TQ = I$.

Key idea: Such a $Q$ is called an **orthogonal matrix**, and its rows are orthonormal too.
cards.searchQuery: orthogonal matrix inverse equals transpose orthonormal columns

cards.title: Why does multiplying by an orthogonal matrix $Q$ preserve lengths?
cards.body:
$\|Q\mathbf{x}\|^2 = (Q\mathbf{x})^T(Q\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^TQ^TQ\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{x} = \|\mathbf{x}\|^2$.

The same computation shows $Q$ **preserves dot products**, hence angles.

Key idea: Taking determinants of $Q^TQ = I$ gives $(\det Q)^2 = 1$, so $\det Q = \pm 1$.
cards.searchQuery: orthogonal matrix preserves length proof

cards.title: $U$ is $m \times n$ with $m > n$ and orthonormal columns. Which is true: $U^TU = I$ or $UU^T = I$?
cards.body:
$U^TU = I_n$, but $UU^T \neq I_m$.

$UU^T$ is the **orthogonal projection** onto $\operatorname{Col}U$, so $UU^T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}$ only for $\mathbf{y}$ in that subspace.

Watch out: $U$ is not square, so it has no inverse.
cards.searchQuery: tall matrix orthonormal columns U transpose U identity

cards.title: An orthogonal projection matrix $P$ onto a subspace $W$ satisfies which two matrix equations?
cards.body:
$P^2 = P$ and $P^T = P$.

**Projecting twice** changes nothing, and orthogonal projections are symmetric.

Key idea: Its eigenvalues are $1$ (on $W$) and $0$ (on $W^\perp$), and $I - P$ projects onto $W^\perp$.
cards.searchQuery: orthogonal projection matrix P squared equals P symmetric

cards.title: In Gram–Schmidt, how is $\mathbf{v}_2$ computed from $\mathbf{x}_2$ and the first vector $\mathbf{v}_1$?
cards.body:
$\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{x}_2 - \dfrac{\mathbf{x}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1}{\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{v}_1$

Subtract the **projection** of $\mathbf{x}_2$ onto $\mathbf{v}_1$, leaving the part orthogonal to $\mathbf{v}_1$.

Key idea: Each later $\mathbf{v}_k$ subtracts the projections onto all of $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_{k-1}$.
cards.searchQuery: Gram-Schmidt formula second orthogonal vector projection

cards.title: Apply Gram–Schmidt to $\mathbf{x}_1 = (1, 0, 1)$ and $\mathbf{x}_2 = (1, 1, 3)$, with $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{x}_1$. What is $\mathbf{v}_2$?
cards.body:
$\mathbf{v}_2 = (-1, 1, 1)$.

$\dfrac{\mathbf{x}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1}{\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1} = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2$, so $\mathbf{v}_2 = (1, 1, 3) - 2(1, 0, 1)$. **Check**: $\mathbf{v}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 = -1 + 0 + 1 = 0$.

Tip: Divide each vector by its length if you need an orthonormal basis.
cards.searchQuery: Gram-Schmidt worked example orthogonal vectors R3

cards.title: In the QR factorization $A = QR$ of a matrix with linearly independent columns, what are $Q$ and $R$?
cards.body:
$Q$ has **orthonormal columns** spanning $\operatorname{Col}A$ (Gram–Schmidt on the columns of $A$, then normalized), and $R$ is upper triangular and invertible, with positive diagonal entries.

Tip: Since $Q^TQ = I$, you can recover $R = Q^TA$.
cards.searchQuery: QR factorization orthonormal columns upper triangular

cards.title: Which equations does a least-squares solution $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ satisfy?
cards.body:
The **normal equations** $A^TA\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^T\mathbf{b}$.

They say that the residual $\mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is orthogonal to every column of $A$.

Key idea: They are always consistent, even when $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is not.
cards.searchQuery: normal equations least squares A transpose A x hat

cards.title: When does $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ have exactly one least-squares solution, and what is it?
cards.body:
When the columns of $A$ are linearly **independent**; then $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{b}$.

Why: Independent columns make $A^TA$ invertible.
Watch out: Otherwise there are infinitely many least-squares solutions, all giving the same $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$.
cards.searchQuery: unique least-squares solution independent columns formula

cards.title: Geometrically, what is $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ when $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is a least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$?
cards.body:
The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto $\operatorname{Col}A$, the point of $\operatorname{Col}A$ **closest** to $\mathbf{b}$.

Key idea: The residual $\mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ lies in $(\operatorname{Col}A)^\perp = \operatorname{Nul}A^T$, and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ minimizes $\|\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}\|$.
cards.searchQuery: least squares solution orthogonal projection onto column space

cards.title: Find the least-squares line $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x$ through the points $(-1, 2)$, $(0, 1)$, $(1, 6)$.
cards.body:
$y = 3 + 2x$.

With rows $(1, x_i)$, $A^TA = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $A^T\mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$, so $\beta_0 = 3$ and $\beta_1 = 2$.

Tip: The **residuals** $(1, -2, 1)$ are orthogonal to both columns of $A$.
cards.searchQuery: least squares line through three points example

cards.title: Given $A = QR$, how do you compute the least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$?
cards.body:
Solve $R\hat{\mathbf{x}} = Q^T\mathbf{b}$ by **back substitution**.

Substituting $A = QR$ into the normal equations gives $R^TR\hat{\mathbf{x}} = R^TQ^T\mathbf{b}$, and $R^T$ is invertible.

Why: This avoids forming $A^TA$, which squares the condition number and loses accuracy.
cards.searchQuery: least squares via QR factorization back substitution

cards.title: $A$ has linearly independent columns. Which matrix projects $\mathbb{R}^m$ orthogonally onto $\operatorname{Col}A$?
cards.body:
$P = A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T$.

It sends $\mathbf{b}$ to $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$, the **least-squares fit**.

Tip: If the columns are orthonormal, $A^TA = I$ and $P$ simplifies to $AA^T$.
cards.searchQuery: projection matrix onto column space formula

cards.title: What does the spectral theorem say about a real symmetric matrix $A$?
cards.body:
$A$ has only real eigenvalues and is **orthogonally diagonalizable**: $A = QDQ^T$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $D$ diagonal.

The columns of $Q$ are orthonormal eigenvectors.

Key idea: Conversely, every matrix $QDQ^T$ is symmetric, so for real matrices, orthogonally diagonalizable means symmetric.
cards.searchQuery: spectral theorem real symmetric matrix orthogonally diagonalizable

cards.title: Why are eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix for distinct eigenvalues orthogonal?
cards.body:
$\lambda_1(\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2) = (A\mathbf{v}_1) \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1 \cdot (A\mathbf{v}_2) = \lambda_2(\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2)$, using $A^T = A$.

Key idea: So $(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)(\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2) = 0$, and $\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2$ **forces** $\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: symmetric matrix eigenvectors distinct eigenvalues orthogonal

cards.title: When is a symmetric matrix $A$ positive definite, and what is the eigenvalue test?
cards.body:
When $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} > 0$ for every $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$; equivalently, when all eigenvalues of $A$ are positive.

Key idea: Positive definite matrices are invertible.
Tip: With $\geq$ in place of $>$ (all eigenvalues $\geq 0$), $A$ is **positive semidefinite**.
cards.searchQuery: positive definite matrix eigenvalue test

cards.title: For which values of $k$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & k \\ k & 8 \end{pmatrix}$ positive definite?
cards.body:
$-4 < k < 4$.

A symmetric $2 \times 2$ matrix is positive definite iff its **top-left entry** is positive ($2 > 0$) and its determinant is positive: $16 - k^2 > 0$.

Watch out: At $k = \pm 4$ the determinant is $0$, so the matrix is only semidefinite.
cards.searchQuery: positive definite 2x2 symmetric matrix parameter k

cards.title: Which symmetric matrix $A$ gives $Q(x, y) = 3x^2 + 4xy + 5y^2$ as $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$?
cards.body:
$A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$

The cross term $4xy$ is **split evenly** between the two off-diagonal entries, because $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ contains $a_{12}xy + a_{21}yx$.

Watch out: Putting $4$ in both spots is the classic mistake.
cards.searchQuery: quadratic form symmetric matrix cross term

cards.title: What is the singular value decomposition of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$?
cards.body:
$A = U\Sigma V^T$, with $U$ ($m \times m$) and $V$ ($n \times n$) orthogonal, and $\Sigma$ ($m \times n$) zero except for $\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq 0$ on its diagonal.

Key idea: The $\sigma_i$ are the **singular values**; the columns of $U$ and $V$ are the left and right singular vectors.
cards.searchQuery: singular value decomposition U Sigma V transpose

cards.title: How are the singular values of $A$ related to the matrix $A^TA$?
cards.body:
They are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^TA$: $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$.

Key idea: $A^TA$ is symmetric with eigenvalues $\lambda_i = \|A\mathbf{v}_i\|^2 \geq 0$, and its orthonormal eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_i$ are the **right singular vectors**.
cards.searchQuery: singular values square roots eigenvalues A transpose A

cards.title: What are the singular values of $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$?
cards.body:
$4$ and $3$.

$A^TA = \begin{pmatrix} 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 16 \end{pmatrix}$, so the singular values are $\sqrt{16}$ and $\sqrt{9}$, listed in **decreasing order**.

Watch out: Singular values are never negative, unlike the eigenvalue $-4$.
Key idea: The rank is the number of nonzero singular values, here $2$.
cards.searchQuery: singular values of a diagonal matrix

cards.title: Given the SVD of $A$, what is the best rank-$k$ approximation to $A$ in the 2-norm or Frobenius norm?
cards.body:
$A_k = \sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{v}_1^T + \cdots + \sigma_k\mathbf{u}_k\mathbf{v}_k^T$: keep the $k$ largest singular values and drop the rest.

Key idea: This is the **Eckart–Young theorem**; the error in the 2-norm is $\sigma_{k+1}$.
Tip: It underlies PCA and image compression.
cards.searchQuery: Eckart-Young best rank k approximation SVD

cards.title: An invertible matrix has largest singular value $50$ and smallest singular value $0.5$. What is its condition number?
cards.body:
$100$.

$\kappa(A) = \sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min} = 50/0.5$ (in the 2-norm).

Watch out: A large $\kappa$ means $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is **ill-conditioned**: a small relative change in $\mathbf{b}$ can change $\mathbf{x}$ by up to $\kappa$ times as much, relatively.
cards.searchQuery: condition number ratio of largest to smallest singular value

cards.title: Which matrices have a singular value decomposition, and which can be diagonalized as $PDP^{-1}$?
cards.body:
**Every matrix**, of any shape, has an SVD; only some square matrices are diagonalizable.

Key idea: The SVD uses two different orthonormal bases ($V$ for inputs, $U$ for outputs), which lets it exist even for $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ or a non-square $A$.
cards.searchQuery: SVD exists for every matrix versus diagonalization
